extracted.intended_audience: public water systems (CWSs and NTNCWSs), State/Tribal governments, regulated entities, stakeholders, and members of the public who will comment on the proposed perchlorate NPDWR
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and statutory requirements for the EPA's proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) and MCL/MCLG for perchlorate, including monitoring, notification, cost‑benefit analysis, and public participation procedures. Useful for entities evaluating applicability, preparing comments, or planning compliance actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDWA regulatory-determination three criteria (1412(b)(1)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish an NPDWR the Administrator must determine that the contaminant: (1) may have an adverse effect on the health of persons; (2) is known to occur or there is a substantial likelihood that the contaminant will occur in PWSs with a frequency and at levels of public health concern; and (3) in the sole judgment of the Administrator, regulation of such a contaminant presents a meaningful opportunity for health risk reductions for persons served by PWSs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three statutory prerequisites are the threshold for making a regulatory determination to regulate a contaminant under SDWA section 1412(b)(1)(A). The preamble repeatedly evaluates perchlorate against these prongs and explains that, absent the D.C. Circuit decision, EPA's science-based analysis would not support regulation because perchlorate is not likely to occur 'with a frequency and at levels of public health concern' and would not present a meaningful opportunity for risk reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) requirement (1412(b)(4)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: An MCLG is the maximum level of a contaminant in drinking water at which no known or anticipated adverse effect on the health of persons would occur, allowing an adequate margin of safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must set an MCLG accompanying a proposed/final NPDWR. In this proposal EPA is proposing an MCLG of 20 µg/L derived from a draft reference dose of 1 μg/kg/day; the MCLG is intended to protect the population at greatest risk (offspring of iodine deficient, hypothyroxinemic women exposed during first trimester). Because the MCLG is set for the most sensitive population it in turn protects the general population consistent with the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting the MCL relative to MCLG and cost‑benefit constraints (1412(b)(4)(B), (b)(6)(A), (b)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: The SDWA generally requires EPA to set the MCL 'as close to the maximum contaminant level goal as is feasible' or, if the Administrator determines the health benefits of the MCL do not justify the cost, at the level where the cost is justified by the benefits, or when it is not economically or technologically feasible to ascertain the level of the contaminant, EPA may issue alternative standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is proposing MCL options at 20, 40, or 80 µg/L and seeks comment on additional MCLs. The Agency explains that although any of the proposed MCLs would be feasible, the Administrator has determined there is no MCL at which benefits of treatment at a limited number of systems justify the costs of monitoring nationwide. When choosing an MCL EPA must balance proximity to the MCLG with feasibility and cost‑justification per the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'feasible' (1412(b)(4)(D)) and feasibility evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Feasible' is defined as 'feasible with the use of the best technology, treatment techniques and other means which the Administrator finds, after examination for efficacy under field conditions and not solely under laboratory conditions, are available (taking cost into consideration).' The means must have been tested beyond the laboratory under full-scale conditions, but need not be in widespread use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In selecting best available technology EPA evaluates the ability to reduce the contaminant, technological and economic feasibility, and historically has defined feasibility relative to what large metropolitan/regional systems can reasonably afford. If no affordable technologies exist for categories of small systems, EPA must identify variance technologies that achieve maximum affordable reduction while protecting health (see SDWA section 1412(b)(15)(A),(B)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Health Risk Reduction and Cost Analysis (HRRCA) requirement (1412(b)(3)(C))
rubrics_metrics.description: In proposing a rule under SDWA, EPA must evaluate quantifiable and nonquantifiable health risk reduction benefits and costs in accordance with the statute's HRRCA requirements, including benefits and costs associated with monitoring, reporting, and mitigation actions. SDWA also requires EPA to determine whether the benefits justify the costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA prepared and references an Economic Analysis (e.g., annualized incremental costs and monetized benefits at 3% and 7% discount rates) and a qualitative summary of non-monetized benefits and costs. The preamble states EPA's current determination that quantified and unquantified benefits of the proposed perchlorate NPDWR do not justify the costs. The HRRCA is subject to public comment and is a substantive element of the rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science Advisory Board consultation prior to proposal (1412(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to proposal of a maximum contaminant level goal and national primary drinking water regulation, EPA must request comments from the Science Advisory Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SDWA section 1412(e) requires SAB consultation; the preamble notes this requirement as part of the statutory steps that must be taken before proposing an NPDWR. Stakeholders can expect scientific peer review opportunities in the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR) and Contaminant Candidate List (CCL) cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress required that once every five years EPA must issue a list of no more than 30 unregulated contaminants to be monitored by PWSs (UCMR) and publish a CCL of contaminants known or anticipated to occur in PWSs. Every five years, after public comment on a preliminary regulatory determination, EPA must issue a determination to regulate or not to regulate at least five contaminants on the CCL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses CCL and UCMR data to assess health effects and occurrence. Perchlorate has been included on multiple CCLs; the preamble explains the statutory cadence and EPA's use of monitoring and occurrence data in regulatory determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping, reporting, and monitoring duties (SDWA section 1445(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person subject to a requirement of SDWA shall establish and maintain records, make reports, conduct monitoring, and provide information to the Administrator as reasonably required by regulation to assist the Administrator in establishing regulations, determining compliance, administering assistance, evaluating risks, and advising the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory provision underpins monitoring/reporting obligations in any final NPDWR and justifies EPA's proposed monitoring, reporting, and compliance framework described elsewhere in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice and notification timing/content requirements (1414(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a final NPDWR is in effect and an MCL is established, SDWA requires PWSs to provide notice to the public if the water system fails to comply with an applicable MCL. The Administrator shall by regulation prescribe the manner, frequency, form, and content for giving notice. For violations with potential for serious adverse effects from short-term exposure, the notice must 'be distributed as soon as practicable, but not later than 24 hours' after the PWS learns of the violation, and the system must report the violation to both the State and the Administrator within that same time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposes that systems issue Tier 1 public notification following an MCL exceedance based on short-term exposure effects on the most sensitive population (here, fetuses of pregnant, hypothyroxinemic, iodine‑deficient women). The preamble cites these statutory timing/content rules as mandatory elements for public notification planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring design and burden-reduction provisions in proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is proposing monitoring, reporting, and other requirements for PWSs to meet the perchlorate MCL. Monitoring frequency of a PWS depends on previous monitoring results. Because most systems are not likely to have perchlorate levels of concern, the proposal includes provisions to reduce burden compared to standard monitoring for other IOCs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions include automatic reductions in monitoring frequency based on initial sampling results and acceptance of previously collected data to satisfy initial monitoring requirements. EPA explains these are intended to reduce burden on systems and States while still identifying systems with perchlorate at/above the MCL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation and comment submission procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit comments identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2024-0592 at https://www.regulations.gov (preferred), or other methods in ADDRESSES. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed. EPA may publish any comment to its public docket. Do not submit CBI/PBI or other restricted disclosure information. Multimedia submissions must be accompanied by a written comment. EPA will generally not consider comments located outside the primary submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points. EPA advises providing written copies of oral testimony and recommends submitting text of oral comments to the docket because oral comments at the hearing may be time-limited. Written statements and supporting information submitted during the comment period will be considered with the same weight as oral comments and supporting information presented at the public hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual public hearing procedures and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will host a virtual public hearing (Feb 19, 2026, ~1–4 p.m. ET). Pre-registration begins upon publication; last day to pre-register to speak is Feb 12, 2026. Online connections are limited and offered first-come, first-served. To submit visual aids, contact NPDWRperchlorate@epa.gov for guidelines by Feb 12, 2026. EPA encourages early registration; oral comments will be time-limited. Accommodations requests (language translation, captioning, special accommodations) must be submitted by Feb 12, 2026.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA will post a general agenda listing pre-registered speakers on Feb 16, 2026. The Agency recommends submitting written copies of oral testimony to the docket. Monitor the Agency website or contact the listed email for hearing updates; EPA does not intend to publish hearing updates in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on withdrawing a prior regulatory determination (effect of NRDC v. Regan)
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Circuit held that EPA lacks authority under SDWA to withdraw a final regulatory determination to regulate a contaminant. Following NRDC v. Regan, EPA cannot finalize an action other than an NPDWR and MCLG where a prior final determination to regulate exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this decision EPA must consider preliminary health benefits analysis information to support the finding that a positive determination would provide a meaningful opportunity for health risk reduction before finalizing a regulatory determination. The preamble states this judicial constraint compelled EPA to propose an NPDWR for perchlorate despite its science-based conclusion that perchlorate does not occur 'with a frequency and at levels of public health concern.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance options and demonstrated treatment technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Water systems with perchlorate levels that exceed the proposed MCL would need to take action to comply. Options include installing water treatment (e.g., ion exchange, reverse osmosis, biological treatment), using a new uncontaminated water source (drilling a new well), or connecting to an uncontaminated water source; certified reverse osmosis point-of-use (POU) devices are available for small systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes these technologies have been demonstrated to remove perchlorate to levels that would comply with proposed MCLs and can be installed at treatment plants; economic analysis references (Economic Analysis section 4.3) provide details on estimating water system costs. Systems exceeding the MCL would also be required to conduct public notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic analysis reporting: incremental costs, benefits, and non-monetized effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The incremental cost of the proposed rule is the difference between quantified costs under the proposed rule and baseline conditions; incremental benefits reflect avoided future adverse health outcomes due to perchlorate reduction. EPA presents annualized incremental costs and monetized annualized incremental benefits for proposed MCLs (20, 40, 80 µg/L) at 3% and 7% discount rates, and notes additional non-monetized benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's reported monetized net annualized incremental benefits are negative for each proposed MCL at both discount rates. The HRRCA should include quantified costs, statistical models, descriptions of unquantifiable costs, and qualitative summaries of monitoring benefits and contaminant removal benefits; the Economic Analysis provides further methodological details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of occurrence and monitoring data in estimating affected systems and populations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses occurrence data (e.g., UCMR results) to estimate the number and share of water systems and people affected by a health reference level or MCL. Past analyses estimated percent of systems and number of people served above HRL/MCL based on sampling data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble references prior use of UCMR 1 occurrence data and describes how EPA estimated systems and populations potentially affected by HRLs. This underlies EPA's assessment that a small percentage of systems have detections above health benchmarks and informs monitoring burdens and cost‑benefit calculations.
